#6017. Mamdani, Hasan Piker among radical left-wing voices erupting over Haley Stevens' endorsement switch

Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers for Senate, saying Abdul El-Sayed made it clear she wasn't welcome in his campaign.

Prominent Democrats and left-wing voices nationwide exploded with fury after Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in the final stretch of Michigan's U.S. Senate race over the weekend.

In her video posted to social media on Sunday after attending church service with Rogers, Stevens noted how Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed told her to "stay away" from his campaign and slammed him for embracing radical steamer Hasan Piker — who was among those criticizing the endorsement.

"Working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday—their healthcare, their rent, their bills," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in an X post. "Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against."

Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said on X shortly after the endorsement: "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."

Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., speaks with media after a debate at WoodTV studios on July 7, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Kristen Norman)

EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT

Stevens, who will leave Congress in January, lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed earlier this year. She was widely viewed as the moderate, establishment candidate compared to the more progressive, left-wing policies of her opponent.

On Sunday, Stevens abandoned the party in the final hours of the Senate campaign as Democrats seek to win back control of the upper chamber.

"This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said on X. "Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors."

DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH

"Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. "We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return."

Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., called Stevens "clearly disturbed," and said she "has thrown her constituents under the bus" on several key midterm issues.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed takes questions from reporters after a campaign rally on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION'

"Too many people live off their 15 minutes of fame," Pocan continued. "In this case, she threw away an entire career because she couldn’t get over a loss and needed attention. Pathetic. Sad. Clearly she has some serious issues. But no one will take her seriously ever again."

Outside of her own colleagues condemning her endorsement, Stevens also saw an immediate staff exodus after she posted the video.

After the endorsement, a visibly upset El-Sayed demanded the media focus their questions on political issues, rather than Stevens' endorsement.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

"I'm going to ask that when we take questions, you keep your questions focused on the issues that Michiganders really care about. Now that might not drive clicks for you. I get it. I understand your business, right? But they're the issues that Michiganders are paying attention to," he said.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and U.S. Senate candidate, during the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY

Stevens drew an official condemnation from the Democratic Party at a national level, too.

"Haley Stevens’ disappointing decision to endorse Mike Rogers, a Trump ally who would join Republican efforts to sell out working families, is a betrayal of the values of the Democratic Party," Democratic National Committee (DNC) chairman Ken Martin said in a statement on behalf of the organization.

"At a moment when Democrats are united in fighting for Michigan families and standing up to Trump’s agenda, we reject these efforts to sow division within our party. We will not allow last-minute political stunts to derail our momentum and we will triple down on our efforts to elect Abdul El-Sayed on Tuesday."

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), chaired by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., lashed out at Stevens' decision, too.

MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED

"The stakes of this election could not be higher: Mike Rogers is a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, and together they plan to continue sowing chaos and making life unaffordable for families while prioritizing their billionaire donors at the expense of Michigan families," the DSCC statement said, adding the group will "reject any efforts to divide Democrats ahead of Tuesday’s crucial election."

DEMOCRAT RIPS HASAN PIKER AS 'HACK WHO THRIVES ON HATE' OVER HIS WARNING TO AMERICAN JEWS ABOUT ISRAEL

Piker, who was partly the reason for Stevens' break from El-Sayed, simply wrote: "i [sic] condemn haley stevens."

Piker has caused major controversy in the Michigan race due to his proximity to El-Sayed. Since his primary win, the progressive candidate has sought to distance himself from the streamer.

"This is the single most unproductive, selfish thing a Democratic candidate has done all cycle and likely many cycles before that," Jon Favreau, Pod Save America cohost and speechwriter to President Barack Obama, said on X. "Having misjudged candidates in the past myself, I hope everyone who tried to recruit, support, and defend Haley can now admit what a mistake it was."

HALEY STEVENS URGES EL-SAYED TO DITCH HASAN PIKER AFFILIATION AFTER MICHIGAN PRIMARY

Fellow PodSaveAmerica cohost Jon Lovett called Stevens a "sleaze."

"Not to downplay Haley Stevens' vermin-like betrayal of her party and her constituents and her nation... But given her track record as a clownish loser, do we really believe any who will now follow her weren't already going to vote for the Fascist?" podcaster and former television sports personality Keith Olbermann said in an X post.

Former President Barack Obama, Abdul El-Sayed and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson raise hands during a campaign event at Cass Technical High School on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

Stevens, who was narrowly defeated by El-Sayed in Michigan's Aug. 4, 2026 primary election, crossed partisan lines after saying for months that she would support El-Sayed.

It all devolved after Stevens expressed concern last week over an ad aired in El-Sayed's favor that was widely viewed as antisemitic. She said she would appear at a weekend campaign event with El-Sayed on the condition that he denounced the ad. El-Sayed, whose support among the Michigan Jewish community is already tenuous, disinvited her from the event instead.

The ad that sparked the controversy was released by the Rebellion PAC, which is operated by The Young Turks co-founder and bombastic leftist commentator Cenk Uygur, who is Piker's uncle. Piker, whom El-Sayed invited onto the campaign trail in Michigan during primary season, has been a headache for El-Sayed during the general election.

Piker said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets, and is known for making antisemitic comments.

El-Sayed has refused to denounce Piker, brushing him off as a "streamer from California" who he says shouldn't be the focus of the campaign in Michigan.

#6016. Fame, Fortune, and Murder in 1960s France

Review: Fame, Fortune, and Murder in 1960s France

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

It helps if you think of the so-called Markovic affair as an accordion. At the beginning, the story is at its thinnest—small and compact. The year is 1968, and a dead body is found, by accident, in a ditch. The corpse is assumed to be that of a vagabond. He receives a half-hearted autopsy—his skull was smashed in, an obvious cause of death—and gets put in the ground.

Still, the judge investigating the case studies the autopsy report and wonders if there is more to it than meets the eye. Would a random, lowly criminal really have perfectly manicured fingernails? A fingerprint match confirms his hunch: The body belonged to Stevan Markovic, an associate of Alain Delon. That’s where Murder in Paris ’68 really picks up.

It helps if you think of the so-called Markovic affair as an accordion. At the beginning, the story is at its thinnest—small and compact. The year is 1968, and a dead body is found, by accident, in a ditch. The corpse is assumed to be that of a vagabond. He receives a half-hearted autopsy—his skull was smashed in, an obvious cause of death—and gets put in the ground.

Murder in Paris ’68: A True Story of Death and Glamour, Edward Chisholm, Pegasus Crime, 416 pp., $32, November 2026

Still, the judge investigating the case studies the autopsy report and wonders if there is more to it than meets the eye. Would a random, lowly criminal really have perfectly manicured fingernails? A fingerprint match confirms his hunch: The body belonged to Stevan Markovic, an associate of Alain Delon. That’s where Murder in Paris ’68 really picks up.

“Associate” is a loose term, but, as author Edward Chisholm explains over the course of roughly 400 pages, it’s better to be vague than incorrect. It’s tough to describe what the two men meant to each other. Markovic was a young man from Yugoslavia who had come to France illegally in hope of a better life. Delon was a movie star, and one of the most beautiful men in the world. They liked and loathed each other, acting as close friends and betraying one another remorselessly. Before his death, Markovic wrote to his brother saying that, if anything were to happen to him, Delon would be “10,000% responsible.”

The scandal following both Markovic’s death centered on this murky and complex relationship. But, according to Chisholm, it had to do with much more than that. The affair was about the nature of fame and fortune in the 1960s, the influence World War II still had on French politics, and a country desperately trying to move toward the future yet weighed down by its heavy past. There was one man at the center of it, sure, but in Chisholm’s telling, you can easily grab the accordion and open it wide, showcasing its countless folds.

Delon with his wife, Nathalie, and their son in Monte Carlo in 1965.Archive Photos via Getty Images

Really, the story begins a decade earlier. In 1955, a 19-year-old Delon left the army after three years. His military record was far from spotless. He spent nearly a third of his time there in prison—for “[o]perating a vehicle without authorization and without a valid licence, resulting in a serious accident,” “[p]ossession of a prohibited weapon,” and “[c]ausing public scandal while ashore,” among other offences. His file concluded that he was “[a] bad element in every respect.”

Now a civilian again, his first port of call was Toulon, in the south of France. He was there to see an old acquaintance, François Marcantoni, a Corsican gangster and former French Resistance fighter who, like many others at the time, moved relentlessly between worlds.

France in the 1950s and 1960s was still fundamentally shaped by the war—by the Nazi occupation and its collaborators in the Vichy government, and by those who fought back. Marcantoni was “arrested in ’44 in a stolen car, running an op for the Resistance. The Gestapo had tortured him,” Chisholm writes. For someone like him, “the post-war years offered two paths: the police, or Pigalle [a neighborhood in Paris]. For François, the choice was obvious. The cops had collaborated, they were the enemy then—and they still were.”

Pigalle was where not-so-reformed Corsican gangsters set up their dodgy bars in the years following the liberation, and where Delon wound up in the late 1950s, when he landed his breakout role in Purple Noon, an adaptation of Patricia Highsmith’s The Talented Mr. Ripley.

A 21-year-old Markovic, meanwhile, made his escape from Josip Broz Tito’s Belgrade to Western Europe in 1958, the same year that Charles de Gaulle, once venerated then cast into the political wilderness, returned to the French presidency.

After a short prison stint in 1965, Markovic, who sustained himself through odd jobs and low-level crime, was in need of a place to stay. His best friend, Milos Milosevic, had managed to befriend Delon a few years earlier while the actor was filming in Belgrade. (Milosevic had staged a fake mugging, before “stepping in” to rescue Delon, and eventually became part of Delon’s entourage.) Milosevic soon convinced Delon to host his friend.

Protest and radicalization are the answer to an authoritarian, centralized state.

François Mitterrand’s U-turn decades ago holds lessons for today.

What happened afterward is complicated. Milosevic died in Hollywood in 1966, in what looked like a murky murder-suicide involving the estranged wife of actor Mickey Rooney. After that, Markovic became an integral part of Delon’s life. As Chisholm explains, Markovic was “[n]ot quite a secretary, not a bodyguard, not an employee. Delon doesn’t pay him—unless you count the occasional envelope. His job is more…ambient.”

“He’s become the man in the background. Pushing the pram through Parc Monceau, driving [Delon’s wife] Nathalie’s Alfa, standing behind the couple at film galas, cocktail in hand,” Chisholm adds. “He’s always there.”

The situation may seem idyllic from the outside; it wasn’t. The nature of the trio’s dynamic was not entirely clear, but the Delons’ marriage was unstable and violent. Sometimes, Markovic felt like he was part of the family; often, the couple put him firmly back in his place. The letters he sent to friends in those years indicate that he was frustrated by this state of affairs, and by Delon’s frequent refusal to sign his residency papers, keeping his legal status irregular.

In 1967, the couple separated. Nathalie moved out, Markovic followed her, and the pair watched as Delon unilaterally announced the divorce on television. What followed was a short-lived affair between the two, which may have sealed his fate.

Markovic’s body was found just over a year later. While much remains unknown, Chisholm makes it clear that the events surrounding the murder cannot be explained without one man: Marcantoni. He was a friend of Delon’s, still, and knew Markovic. He spent the 1960s arguing that he was no longer a gangster—retired long ago—and merely a “victim of [his] reputation,” which few people bought even then. He’s mentioned by name in the infamous letter Markovic sent to his brother. Was he a murderer?

The book alleges that he is (it can afford to—Marcantoni died in 2010), but the murder was never solved. There are, Chisholm explains, four prevailing theories. The first is that Delon had Markovic killed for sleeping with his wife, probably enlisting Marcantoni’s help. The second is that Markovic planned to sell stories and pictures of the Delons, but they found out and had him killed, likely with Marcantoni. The third is that Markovic’s personal dealings with the underworld got him killed, possibly by Marcantoni, possibly by someone else.

The fourth—watch as the accordion expands—is that, through his association with the Delons, Markovic had made his way into the upper echelons of French society, where politicians, singers, actors, and high-end criminals partied and slept together in secret. Could the young Yugoslav have gone to those events, taking covert pictures of the Parisian elite in compromising positions? We know now that no evidence exists (or remains) of this, but the theory tantalized France for months after his death.

Most shocking of all were snaps that emerged of a woman engaged in a tryst with another woman, which made their way to the Parisian police. The woman was believed to be Claude, the wife of Prime Minister Georges Pompidou. These were so obviously doctored that they did not even become a part of the police investigation, but the story was too salacious to die quietly. De Gaulle, aging, tired, did little to protect the man who had been faithfully at his side since his return to the Élysée Palace a decade earlier. Meanwhile, political opponents, hungry journalists, and at least one Czech spy conspired to ensure that the Pompidou name would keep being embroiled in the Markovic affair.

It helped Marcantoni, as the main suspect, that this merry band of interested parties was invested in turning the story into a political scandal. In 1969, he was arrested and held in custody after investigators had traced the plastic in which the body had been wrapped to packaging used by a mattress brand that Marcantoni had in his house. He spent just under a year behind bars, then left a free man. With no one talking, there just wasn’t enough there for a conviction.

Though the case rumbled on after that, the Markovic affair was essentially over. France had turned a new leaf too. The riots of May ’68, which had united students, workers, and millions of others in protesting for a brighter future, had initially failed to remove de Gaulle from his post. But a year later, despite the success of his party and the support of figures including Delon, de Gaulle resigned. Pompidou, a man who did not fight during the war and whose love of contemporary art and friendships in the entertainment world shocked his predecessors, took his place. Finally, the future of France was taking form. Everyone was moving on.

Marcantoni, now free for good, published multiple books concerning the affair, including the provocatively titled But Who Killed Markovic?. He became famous for claiming that “only three people know the truth. Delon, me and God. And God never snitches.” Delon died two years ago, and though his career continued for decades after the murder, it largely peaked in the 1960s. Maybe there was a reason he supported de Gaulle and not the idealist youths in 1968. On some level, he knew that, despite being in his early 30s, he could only ever be part of the old guard.

Delon (center) leaves court in Versailles in 1973.AFP via Getty Images

That is the book’s thesis anyway. Much of Murder in Paris ’68 tries to convince us that the affair was, in some way, about all of human life. “At first, I thought this was a story about a murder,” Chisholm writes. “Then it became a story about cinema. Then politics, espionage, a cover-up. But somewhere along the way, it became something else. A story about power. About what happens when someone tries to become more than they are allowed to be.”

This is one way to interpret it, but it is equally easy to read Chisholm’s yarn and come to another conclusion altogether. Delon was a cold, unpleasant man with a large ego who relished the company of outlaws. His wife was young, unreliable, and prone to follow her husband’s lead in toying with those she deemed beneath her. Many of the people they socialized with were either low-level swindlers or hardened criminals, always looking to make a quick buck.

Markovic was a man who got lucky and unlucky; who cheated and stole his way through life, then, for a short while, found himself attached to a man who happened to be a god. Always, he returned to what he knew: petty, lazy crime. It’s possible to squint and follow Chisholm in comparing him to Brutus or Iago—Shakespeare’s second men—but, really, he may have just been a minor crook who died in the way minor crooks sometimes did in those days.

By dragging Markovic’s lifeless body back in the spotlight today, Chisholm has merely become the latest in a long line of people, from Pompidou’s detractors to Marcantoni’s publishers, willing to use him for their own ends. It makes for a compelling read, though you should remember that, even as an accordion is at its widest, it’s only ever full of air.

#6014. Putin’s Strategy Is Working

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MICHAEL MCFAUL is Professor of Political Science, a Senior Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute, and a Hoover Fellow at Stanford University. He served as Ambassador to Russia from 2012 to 2014 and is the author of Autocrats vs. Democrats: China, Russia, America, and the New Global Disorder.

Trump Could Salvage the Kremlin’s Objectives in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin plays the long game. For decades, the Russian leader has worked to subjugate Ukraine. For decades, he has also cultivated ties with Donald Trump. Now, success at the latter endeavor is allowing Putin to recover from failures at the former: after nearly five years of thwarted Russian objectives in the war on Ukraine, the U.S. president is helping him win. By easing sanctions on Russia, cutting military and economic assistance to Ukraine, disrupting intelligence cooperation, and pressuring Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to accept Putin’s war aims, Trump is making Russia’s successful annexation of substantial Ukrainian territory and de facto control over Kyiv’s future decisions more likely than at almost any point since February 2022.

Since Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, battlefield momentum has swung back and forth between the two sides. Russian forces had the advantage at the start. But by the fall of 2022, Ukraine had seized the offensive, liberating so much territory once held by Russian troops that Washington worried Putin might use a nuclear weapon to stop Ukrainian advances. The war then settled into a tragic grind on the frontline—until last spring. Momentum returned to Ukraine after Kyiv deployed new long-range missiles capable of striking targets deep inside Russia, new midrange drones able to attack Russian supply routes in the occupied parts of eastern Ukraine, and improved interceptor drones that could better defend against Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. Putin’s army proved unable to advance on the frontline; Ukrainian troops even made incremental progress in liberating territory.

But Trump has helped return the momentum to Russia. Stymied at the frontline, Putin has shifted his focus to terrorizing Ukrainian society through rocket and drone strikes on both civilians and the infrastructure their livelihood depends on—energy and water in particular—driven by the hope that a suffering population would pressure Zelensky to capitulate. New weaponry has made this terrorist campaign especially brutal, in particular the mass production of ballistic missiles and a new drone, the Geran 5, equipped with a powerful Chinese rocket engine that Ukrainian air defenses cannot intercept. Because Russia has more troops, greater military production capacity, and some new and better weapons, Putin believes that he can afford to persist despite the seeming stalemate.

Trump’s support has bolstered Putin’s belief that time is on his side. In just the last few weeks, Trump and his allies have expanded his help to Moscow: suspending sanctions, buying Russian diesel, disrupting Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield communications systems, and even insisting that Zelensky must go. “It is equally clear that when some partners ease the pressure on Russia,” Zelensky has noted, “it only reinforces Putin’s belief that his goals are within reach.” The combination of less support from the United States, especially when it comes to air defenses, and faster Russian drones and more missiles will make the coming winter the most brutal yet for Ukrainians.

Putin’s long game with Trump began years ago, driven not so much by some specific objective, but by the hope that Kremlin influence on him might someday prove useful—a common KGB tactic. Now that day has come.

Years before Trump first ran for president, Russian actors close to Putin pursued business ties with the then real estate mogul, including most famously when Trump collaborated with Emin and Aras Agalarov to host the Miss Universe pageant in Moscow in 2013. Putin then orchestrated unprecedented foreign interference in the 2016 presidential election to help Trump and hurt his opponent Hillary Clinton. Whether the Russian theft and publication of Clinton campaign emails, combined with a comprehensive social media effort to bolster Trump, affected the 2016 election outcome is impossible to prove. That Putin was trying to influence the result is without question.

In 2017, Putin’s cultivation of Trump started to deliver some atmospheric benefits. Trump made clear his admiration for the Russian dictator. More shockingly, during his summit with Putin in Helsinki in 2018, Trump expressed doubt about the findings of his intelligence community regarding Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and instead endorsed Putin’s denial. Yet in his first term, Trump’s rhetorical adulation of Putin only marginally changed actual U.S. policy toward Russia, in part because several senior officials on Trump’s national security team—National Security Adviser H. R. McMaster, Secretary of Defense James Mattis, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo—constrained Trump from making a full pro-Russia pivot.

After Trump’s reelection, in 2024, the Kremlin’s long courtship started to produce more tangible results. Most consequentially, Trump ended direct U.S. military and economic assistance to Ukraine. Before then, the United States was Ukraine’s biggest backer. Trump has still allowed American companies to sell some arms to European governments, who then transfer them to Ukraine. But even that channel has been disrupted periodically and only amounts to a trickle of weapons and ammunition compared with what the United States previously provided. And what Ukraine needs most—interceptors for its Patriot missile defense systems—are in very short supply, in part because the United States has launched so many of them during Trump’s war with Iran.

Other U.S. steps have further undermined Ukraine and aided Russia. Trump has insisted that Ukraine would never join NATO. He gave Putin red-carpet treatment at an Alaska summit last year, at which the two presidents talked about pressuring Ukraine to give up the rest of the eastern region of the Donbas, which Putin has been trying to conquer since 2014. Trump has periodically berated Zelensky, including most dramatically at a February 2025 Oval Office meeting, when he cut off Zelensky and yelled, “You’ve done enough talking. You’re not winning this . . . You don’t have the cards.” Since then, Trump has occasionally zagged back to more cordial relations with the Ukrainian president. But Trump has returned to expressing open hostility, echoing Putin by proclaiming that it’s “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

In the last two weeks, Trump has increased support for Putin’s war. He lifted sanctions to allow the sale of Russian diesel exports, which will provide Moscow with billions of dollars to help finance military operations. He issued an executive order suspending new sanctions outlined in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he had signed just weeks earlier. There have been new lapses in sharing certain kinds of intelligence that only the United States can provide. Most consequentially, Ukraine has experienced disruptions in its access to Starlink and Starshield communications systems provided by SpaceX (a company owned by Elon Musk, a major backer and ally of Trump and a former official in his administration). Kyiv needs both services to guide its own drones and to track and defend against Russian drones and rockets. Whether the U.S. government or Musk independently ordered the disruptions is still not clear. But the results of the disruptions were clear: more Russian drones and rockets hit more Ukrainian targets, including innocent civilians; more Russian weaponry moved closer to the frontline; and more Ukrainian drones fell out of the air.

Through their teams, Putin and Trump have also been negotiating new business deals, including the purchase of assets owned by a major Russian oil company, Lukoil, by American investors; the sale of a currently dormant gas pipeline, Nord Stream 2, connecting Germany and Russia; and even secret Russian investments in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska. If they move forward, all these projects will provide Putin with new revenues to underwrite his war in Ukraine.

Ukrainians are not giving up; according to polls, a solid majority still think that their country should keep fighting. Nor are Europeans quitting on Ukraine. Although Putin hoped that the withdrawal of American military and economic aid early in Trump’s second term would lead to a quick Ukrainian collapse or capitulation, he did not anticipate how willing and capable European countries would be in filling the American void. What’s more, Ukrainian defense tech companies are working frantically to develop new weapons to intercept the rapidly rising number of Russian ballistic missiles and speedy Geran 5 drones. Right now, the pendulum has swung in Russia’s direction, but the Ukrainians have defied expectations and regained momentum many times in the past; they can do it again.

U.S. policy could also change, especially after the midterm elections. American society does not support Trump’s embrace of Putin and abandonment of Ukraine, making it politically hard for the administration to maintain this policy pivot. If Democrats win control of one or both houses of Congress in midterm elections next week, they could very well use their new electoral mandate to investigate American-Russian business deals; introduce new legislation to restart American military and economic assistance to Ukraine and outlaw Starlink and Starshield disruptions; or deploy legislative action to enforce existing sanctions laws. Even Trump himself has stepped back from Putin before—he once wondered out loud whether Putin was “tapping me along.” He could do so again.

Putin should also realize that his cultivation of Trump is a wasting asset. No future president—Democrat or Republican—is likely to continue Trump’s Russia policy. And next week, Trump will become a lame duck, whose power to shape U.S. policy toward Russia will decline over the next two years. Putin would be wise, accordingly, to get serious about negotiating a cease-fire now. His odds of getting a favorable deal will only diminish from here.

#6013. Supreme Court denies Trump admin request to reverse block on segregating 20K California ballots

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter joins 'Saturday in America' to weigh in on the Justice Department investigation into alleged illegal voting in California.

The U.S. Supreme Court (SCOTUS) on Monday rejected a Trump administration request to temporarily block lower-court rulings that denied requests to segregate more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots cast by people it says are likely not U.S. citizens.

Justice Elena Kagan denied the appeal on the eve of the midterm elections without comment, and did not refer it to the other justices.

The administration argued that the limited injunction would preserve the ballots while their eligibility is investigated, without canceling any votes. California and the federal government dispute whether the ballots are unlawful.

"Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm is impossible to remedy," the Department of Justice (DOJ) wrote in a court filing.

JUDGE REJECTS DOJ REQUEST TO BLOCK CALIFORNIA FROM IMMEDIATELY COUNTING BALLOTS LINKED TO ALLEGED NONCITIZENS

California has a heavy Democratic registered voter edge over Republicans and has the highest representation in the House with 52 seats, mostly Democratic. (Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images; Emily Elconin/Reuters)

The SCOTUS appeal came about after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the request Friday, with Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting, as did a federal judge in Los Angeles last week.

The DOJ sought relief while the matter proceeds. California says its safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and argues the federal list may contain errors that could disenfranchise eligible voters.

The lower courts also cited the state’s authority over election procedures and warned that granting the request could jeopardize the election.

On Monday evening, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., said it was "likely" the Trump administration violated the Constitution by taking over responsibilities for elections from the states and Congress.

Chief Judge James Boasberg issued an injunction blocking the administration from making requests from California over its mail-in ballots.

DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS

The case stems from an Oct. 15 DOJ lawsuit alleging that California is impeding enforcement of a federal law barring noncitizens from voting in federal elections.

The administration says the state violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which generally gives federal law precedence over state law.

The dispute comes amid the administration’s broader push to influence how states run elections, including demands for access to voter rolls and warnings that officials could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote.

California, the nation’s most populous state, has 52 House seats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.

Fox News' Shannon Bream and Bill Mears and Reuters contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

#6011. AI Isn’t a Revolution—Yet

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: AI Isn’t a Revolution—Yet

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

For a time, in the 1980s, the Industrial Revolution lost its status as a “revolution.” New quantitative measures threatened to demote Britain’s 18th-century economic transformation to the status of an unglamorous, long-term “process.” It simply unfolded too slowly and in too few sectors to justify terminology implying total, overnight transformation.

Ultimately, the Industrial Revolution was rehabilitated as a “revolution”—albeit with the recognition that it was more gradual and uneven than the word traditionally implies. The question in this scholarly debate was never whether the steam engine was revolutionary, because people and institutions determine whether a potentially game-changing invention turns out to have truly revolutionary impact. A key factor in the Industrial Revolution’s slow unfolding was British people’s active resistance to changes instigated by steam power and factory organization—to an extent that shook posterity’s very certainty of its standing as a “revolution.”

For a time, in the 1980s, the Industrial Revolution lost its status as a “revolution.” New quantitative measures threatened to demote Britain’s 18th-century economic transformation to the status of an unglamorous, long-term “process.” It simply unfolded too slowly and in too few sectors to justify terminology implying total, overnight transformation.

Ultimately, the Industrial Revolution was rehabilitated as a “revolution”—albeit with the recognition that it was more gradual and uneven than the word traditionally implies. The question in this scholarly debate was never whether the steam engine was revolutionary, because people and institutions determine whether a potentially game-changing invention turns out to have truly revolutionary impact. A key factor in the Industrial Revolution’s slow unfolding was British people’s active resistance to changes instigated by steam power and factory organization—to an extent that shook posterity’s very certainty of its standing as a “revolution.”

CEOs of AI companies who cry that their technology is too intrinsically revolutionary to handle and that they must therefore be exempted from accountability to antitrust and product liability regulations exploit the U.S. public’s loose grasp of this historical truth: that it (and the wider global public) has an enormous role in deciding whether a technology is revolutionary.

Though working-class British people lacked the right to vote and unions were barely legal when steam power appeared, with their organizing efforts they both slowed the technology’s spread and ensured they had some say in setting the terms of its use through laws regulating workers’ hours, safety, and age. They rioted and broke machines, they created underground unions, held mass public gatherings, petitioned and marched, wrote and printed pamphlets. They presented such a threat to the oligarchy that the government spared massive amounts of troops to suppress them even as it fought Napoleon around the world.

They persisted because the stakes were enormous: an entire way of life. A way of life in which work and life were not sharply differentiated, in which customs of trade assured standards of craftsmanship, just prices, and fair wages, and in which those who were not wealthy still had self-respect and a sense of independence. Many ordinary Britons experienced the Industrial Revolution’s threat to this way of life as a violence to human nature worth shedding blood over.

A drawing depicts Luddites destroying textile machines in the United Kingdom circa 1811. API/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images

Though the term “Luddite” has become an epithet for the irrational rejection of new technology, the machine-wrecking Luddites of the 1810s were not fighting power looms themselves but the exploitative and oppressive relationships governing factory owners’ adoption of them. A tax on power looms, for instance, would have helped equalize competition and fund relief for displaced handloom weavers.

“What was at issue,” the historian E. P. Thompson explained in the 1960s, “was the ‘freedom’ of the capitalist to destroy the customs of the trade, whether by new machinery, by the factory-system, or by unrestricted competition, beating-down wages, undercutting his rivals, and undermining standards of craftsmanship … [T]he ‘free’ factory-owner … who built his fortune by these means, was regarded … as a man engaging in immoral and illegal practices.” To ordinary Britons, laissez-faire capitalism was not freedom but a “foul Imposition”: no “natural law” permitted a man to engage in practices that injured fellow men. The Luddites didn’t look only backward but also forward to a new, democratic industrial society in which pursuit of profit would be subordinated to ethical priorities and collective needs.

The CEOs’ framing of AI as an unstoppable force that will inevitably transform everything overnight exploits the popular understanding of the Industrial Revolution as an overnight transformation caused by the invention of steam power by unfettered geniuses—a fable generated by liberal, and neoliberal, political economic theory. When devotees of this theory do recognize the Industrial Revolution’s slowness, they take that pace for granted as its intrinsic nature, rather than the contingent product of the agency of masses of dispossessed people. Thus, the economist Daron Acemoglu sees our times as “unprecedented,” because “the first phase of the Industrial Revolution lasted for 80 years. Today it’s taking place in one or two years … across many sectors at the same time.” Though helpfully warning of the risks posed by AI, Acemoglu blinds himself to the useful precedent of resistance behind the seeming dissimilarity of the Industrial Revolution.

We have not suddenly departed from set norms of economic transformation; no such laws of history guide the march of economic and technological progress. Britain’s Industrial Revolution in fact depended greatly on government military contracts, just as military contracts drove the Cold War rise of Silicon Valley and have proved critical for the development of AI itself. Technological leaps are not the result of some inexorable historical process; they have been the product of intentional, high-risk investment in innovation made possible by the vast resources of powerful governments. The U.S. government’s passivity toward the harms of AI companies’ products—its ongoing failure to enforce existing laws against distribution of defective and harmful products—is yet another way it is accelerating the spread of AI.

AI companies, the U.S. government, and liberal myths about history have thus set AI up to be disruptive—to be revolutionary in its impact. And it will be, so long as the U.S. public succumbs to the CEOs’ claims about how technological revolutions happen and fails to recognize its capacity to contain them—as ordinary British people reined in the Industrial Revolution. The CEOs’ framing of AI as inherently revolutionary helps elicit special favors from the government and discourage public pushback. The government’s partnership with these companies thus far means that it will not hold them accountable on its own. Public pressure is required.

Indeed, the public has been involved from the outset as the taxpayers who fund the government’s contracts; they can and should demand a role in the development of AI going forward and reprise their past role in asserting democratic oversight over disruptive technologies.

Protesters take part in a “Stop the AI Race” demonstration calling for a slowdown in the development of advanced artificial intelligence systems, seen outside City Hall in San Francisco on Sept. 17.Karl Mondon/AFP via Getty Images

This is not a genie-can’t-be-put-back-in-the-bottle situation. The European Union in 2024 passed laws prohibiting AI systems that threaten human safety and rights, which have already slowed the rollout of AI products there. U.S. policymakers must at the very least apply existing regulations for protecting against environmentally harmful and defective products to AI. Taxpayers must also demand that the government use the leverage of its reputation-enhancing contracts to insist AI companies prioritize the safety of their products over the reckless expansion of those products’ capacities.

Making such demands does not automatically hand disruptive power to China, whose AI products would be held to the same standards and regulations for use in the United States (where many companies already use Chinese open models). The nuclear non-proliferation deals the United States brokered with its arch enemy, the Soviet Union, at the height of the Cold War are historical proof of the possibility of limiting the spread of dangerous technologies through global cooperation.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”

A global boom is underway. Are countries ready?

Talk of “super intelligence” distracts from frequent screwups.

But effective pushback requires organizing and effort beyond what a citizenry trained to express itself only through the vote is accustomed to. It requires new kinds of unions in new kinds of workplaces, and old kinds of crowd action. It requires shifting pension investments away from these companies. It requires supporting coalitions of concerned AI scientists—and ensuring no AI CEO hijacks calls for new regulations to propose laws that exempt their products from ordinary liability (such as Anthropic’s draft bill that would allow the government to block its models only if there’s potential for $1 billion in damages, or more than 50 people are at risk of being killed or injured). It means suing companies that release unsafe AI products when their corporate allies fail to, as one nonprofit has now done for the OpenAI hack into Hugging Face.

Public insistence on accountability is clearly effectual—OpenAI has paused the release of its latest model due to security concerns. But the public must organize even without a guarantee that their efforts will succeed. Resistance didn’t stop the Industrial Revolution, but it did slow it down, and that mattered to the generations who lived through it. It also ensured that British workers’ living standards ultimately rose. More importantly, within their collective organizations, ordinary Britons reclaimed the dignity and humanity that they were fighting for. As catastrophic as their sufferings were during the Industrial Revolution, the craftsmen resisting its harms produced what Thompson called “the most distinguished popular culture England has known,” yielding countless inventors, organizers, journalists, and political theorists, and a vision of a new kind of democratic society.

Likewise, in resuming their historic struggle against oligarchic exploitation, Americans stand to gain much culturally and socially, quite apart from the impact they might have on stopping the spread of harmful AI products: These very activities offer the chance at recovering dignity, equity, independence—humanness itself.

The American public will decide whether there is an “AI revolution.”

This post appeared in the FP Weekend newsletter, a weekly showcase of book reviews, deep dives, and features. Sign up here.

Priya Satia is the Raymond A. Spruance professor of international history at Stanford University and the award-winning author of Spies in Arabia: The Great War and the Cultural Foundations of Britain’s Covert Empire in the Middle East and Empire of Guns: The Violent Making of the Industrial Revolution. Her most recent book is Time’s Monster: How History Makes History.

#6009. How to Secure the Straits

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DANA STROUL is Director of Research at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. She served as U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for the Middle East from February 2021 to December 2023.

Why Iran and the Houthis Keep Winning the Waterways

Over the past month, Iran has made its most intense attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel declared war, in February. More than 100 drone and missile launches into the strait have been recorded since the war began; in October alone, a container ship and a bulk vessel sank in the waterway. Meanwhile, in the Red Sea, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have sustained their campaign to throttle seaborne trade as they target Saudi Arabia more directly, seizing new territory along the Bab el Mandeb Strait.

These dual maritime crises form part of the same strategic problem—one that, despite its new intensity, has existed for years. In 2019, Iran attacked shipping across the Gulf in response to the first Trump administration’s maximum-pressure sanctions campaign; in 2023, the Houthis launched assaults in the Red Sea following Hamas’s October 7 massacre in Israel. After each of these campaigns, the United States and its partners established maritime coalitions to protect these vital seaborne trade routes. The efforts helped secure the waterways, but they never fundamentally persuaded Iran and its proxies that asymmetric attacks on shipping were an ineffective way to project power. On the contrary, such tactics have only become more appealing to Tehran.

Even now, some shipping persists through both waterways. On October 15, Lloyd’s List Intelligence reported that transit through the Bab el Mandeb Strait was up modestly from August. U.S. naval patrols—as well as creative logistical adaptation by Gulf states, including ship-to-ship transfers, have allowed some oil to move through Hormuz. But shipping still remains throttled, and international actors have not yet found a way to update their deterrence playbook. In 2019 and 2023–24, U.S., European, and Middle Eastern navies formed separate, overlapping defensive maritime coalitions to escort vessels, collect intelligence on evolving threats, and intercept missile and drone attacks. In the United States’ case in 2024, a separate multinational coalition also conducted offensive strikes in Yemen to undermine Houthi maritime capabilities. Today, governments are falling back on the same instinct—to join forces, but not all their forces. The British and the French have proposed a multinational maritime defense coalition to secure the Strait of Hormuz once the war ends, while Saudi Arabia is planning, but has not yet deployed, its own alliance to protect the Red Sea. Neither project includes the United States, which has deployed nearly one-third of its naval warships to the Middle East in an attempt to reestablish freedom of navigation, enforce a naval blockade against Iran, and support U.S. attacks on Iran.

Multiple short-term, insufficiently coordinated defensive missions organized around voluntary contributions can buy down marginal risk for shippers in the near-term but they cannot deliver long-term deterrence. Separate missions embolden Iranian and Houthi leaders, who will interpret them as half-measures that are easily strained by resource scarcity, an inability to adapt quickly to evolving threats, and the absence of real-time intelligence sharing across the two chokepoints. As crises in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea become more linked amid an expanding regional war, replicating the patchwork maritime strategy that never fully worked would be a serious mistake. What is needed instead is a single, sustained multinational effort to secure both waterways that combines American military capabilities with the imprimatur of a unified coalition of Asian, European, and Middle Eastern countries. Otherwise, Iran and the Houthis will again learn that threatening global commerce in maritime chokepoints is a strategy worth repeating.

The maritime coalitions now taking shape share a troubling precedent. Twice before, international actors have mounted similar efforts, and their mixed results show why even effective defensive operations fail to prevent renewed attacks in Middle Eastern waterways. In mid-2019, after the first Trump administration launched its “maximum pressure” sanctions campaign against Iran, Tehran attacked tankers off the coast of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and in the Gulf of Oman and seized a British-flagged oil tanker from international waters in the Strait of Hormuz. Insurance premiums spiked tenfold, and freight rates for crude-oil-carrying tankers jumped nearly 40 percent. In response, Washington established the International Maritime Security Construct (IMSC), headquartered in Bahrain; the mission sought to maintain naval vessels across key waterways in the Middle East to deter Iran and collect intelligence on Iranian maritime activities to share with commercial shippers.

By the end of 2019, Albania, Australia, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and the United Kingdom had joined the IMSC. But despite Washington’s efforts to expand the coalition further, most European countries abstained from joining. They were frustrated with the Trump administration’s withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear deal with Tehran and wary that joining the IMSC—with its focus on confronting Iran—would be seen by Tehran as aggressive or an endorsement of Washington’s maximum pressure campaign. Instead, eight European countries joined a French-led mission called European Maritime Awareness in the Strait of Hormuz (EMASoH), which emphasized de-escalation, surveillance, and encouraging regional dialogue with Iran.

Four years later, when the Houthis began to threaten shipping in the Red Sea—spiking maritime insurance rates and forcing vessels to detour around the Cape of Good Hope—the United States and Europe once again organized separate responses. In December 2023, the United States launched Operational Prosperity Guardian (OPG), a naval coalition soon joined by more than 20 countries. The mission maintained four to eight warships in the Red Sea area at any given time and successfully shot down Houthi drones and missiles; within its first month, its leaders said it had facilitated safe transit for more than a thousand commercial vessels. The European Union formed its own, substantially smaller defensive maritime operation that escorted European commercial vessels through the southern Red Sea and also intercepted Houthi drone and missile attacks.

In both crises, the United States, Europe, and the Gulf states broadly agreed that Iranian and Houthi threats to freedom of navigation required a response. Because freedom of navigation was viewed as a fundamental principle of the global order, assembling large groups committed to upholding this pillar was intended to demonstrate international resolve and isolate the bad actor. But disagreement over how to confront the challenge diluted the missions. Many governments declined to join offensive strikes or coalitions explicitly directed at a state. Political divides further splintered the response, as Europe sought to put distance between itself and the United States’ Iran strategy.The 2019–24 missions achieved important tactical successes by improving maritime awareness, intercepting some attacks, and stopping a complete shutdown of shipping. But the lack of a long-term, coordinated strategy for ending Iran’s aggression weakened the response. The missions never fully persuaded shippers that these waterways were safe—especially the Red Sea—or prevented Iran and the Houthis from eventually returning to their efforts to exploit the chokepoints. According to a 2021 assessment by the Dutch government, the Netherlands assumed that Iran could differentiate between the European maritime mission and the American-led one and would be less aggressive toward European vessels, underscoring Tehran’s ability to exploit the gaps between overlapping operations and the need for a unified front.

The lessons from these missions matter enormously today. After years of shadow warfare, the United States and Israel have now fought Iran directly. In 2025, the United States and Israel also launched separate months-long campaigns against the Houthis in Yemen, following a decadelong Saudi-led effort to dislodge the rebel group. These campaigns badly battered Iran and the Houthis. But they also gave them a chance to hone their asymmetric tactics. Having survived wars intended to collapse their regimes, Iran and the Houthis have emerged more willing to hold global commerce at risk and impose costs on actors not directly involved in the wars against them. Both have learned that they do not need to fully close maritime chokepoints. Simply threatening them can change decision-making in the halls of power.

Nobody wants tolls or unilaterally imposed service payments on these waterways, proposals that Iran has tabled. Instead, to try to deal with the crises, there has been a flowering of disjointed maritime coalition planning efforts. The British-French plan resembles previous European maritime efforts, proposing a defensive multinational mission to escort vessels. It excludes the United States and will not activate until the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran ends for good—a condition that essentially guarantees its uselessness in the near term. Houthi aggression, meanwhile, has sent Saudi Arabia scrambling to secure Red Sea transit, which is increasingly vital given disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. In late July, Riyadh announced the formation of its own defensive maritime coalition with 14 countries from across Africa and the Middle East, as well as Bangladesh and Pakistan, which will be distinct from both European efforts on Hormuz and the U.S. mission. The United States has put up its own military effort to secure Gulf waterways focused on escorting vessels through Omani waters and actively defending commercial shippers from daily Iranian attacks. Concurrently, the U.S. Navy is enforcing a naval blockade against Iranian ports and disabling tankers that ignore its warnings.

The European and Saudi plans are already behind the curve of events. Leaders across Europe and the Middle East want to differentiate their defensive maritime missions from U.S. and Israeli offensive campaigns against Iran in order to prevent escalation and protect their own forces. But the European and Saudi efforts have not moved beyond planning. The U.S. mission, for its part, is active in the wartime waterways of the Middle East and has for now successfully restored much of the prewar crude oil flows out of the region amid Iranian attacks. But eventually, the U.S. Navy will struggle to maintain its large presence in the Middle East given competing priorities and the wear and tear of continuous deployment. Iranian leaders are gambling that they can outlast the United States in will and capability, while driving wedges between Washington and its long-standing partners in Asia, Europe, and the Middle East, who have yet to meaningfully defend maritime transit. These coalitions will all fail to deter Iran and the Houthis for good if they do not coordinate with each other.

Without American naval capabilities and intelligence, maritime missions to secure these waterways simply cannot succeed given the scope and scale of the threat. (In 2019, the European mission was only able to field a maximum of three warships and a single patrol aircraft, compared with the United States’ dozen ships; the United States’ 2023–24 OPG mission was able to respond thanks to its naval bases nearby in Bahrain.) Yet U.S. naval superiority itself is insufficient. Iran and the Houthis have seen this rush to uncoordinated maritime coalitions before, and they know how to exploit the political and operational gaps. Truly isolating Iran is the best way to win concessions from its leaders. Both it and the Houthis have little reason to abandon their tactics if governments cannot agree on how to confront them.

European and Saudi leaders need to merge their maritime planning efforts and invite the United States to join. Whatever serious disagreements they have with Washington about its military actions in Iran must be set aside when it comes to confronting the throttling of international waterways. An Arab- and European-led command structure, supported by American military capabilities, would demonstrate broad international opposition to maritime aggression while distinguishing the mission from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iranian territory.

For now, the United States should be prepared to contribute significant military capacity and operational support, given the extensive deployments it already has in the Middle East. Its partners across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East should redirect the resources they pledged to the European and Saudi missions to a broader coalition that includes the United States. And Washington must lean into a role as military integrator, smoothing out communication and coordination at sea for navies not used to dynamic multimember missions. In particular, the United States and Israel must share real-time intelligence about the evolving nature of Iranian and Houthi targeting capabilities and weapons, so that maritime coalition members can get ahead of the innovation curve.

In the near term, the United States should commit to operational flexibility, seconding any offensive strikes to a separate chain of command. Leaders in Tehran will take notice of a unified international response to Iranian and Houthi maritime aggression and will think twice before attacking a mission made up of dozens of navies all working together. In return, Washington must accept that its partners would be joining a defensive maritime mission—not enforcing the naval blockade or entering the war against Iran. In 2024, Washington took care to differentiate its role in the OPG defensive Red Sea mission from the separate multinational offensive strikes it undertook against the Houthis. The U.S. government should replicate that model today.

Other militaries, including Israel’s, should contribute intelligence, sea drones and other unmanned capabilities,maintenance and logistical support, and personnel. In return for the United States serving as the mission’s backbone, European, Middle Eastern, and Asian partners should commit to gradually expanding their own naval capabilities and assets so the coalition becomes a long-term investment with equitably shared burdens. Joint messaging—regular coordinated statements and outreach to commercial shippers to counter Iranian and Houthi disinformation—will be vital, as well as collaborative innovation. Iran and the Houthis adapt rapidly; it will be easier for coalition countries’ defense industries to stay ahead of them if they work together.

Military efforts to date have failed to compel either Iran or the Houthis to change course at sea. In fact, Iranian and Houthi leaders believe that they have more to gain from escalation, as evidenced by their statements and continued attacks. Countries everywhere are suffering for it. In October, the World Bank projected that Gulf economies would contract by 4.3 percent in 2026, thanks in no small part to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure. In June, the International Monetary Fund estimated that the war in Iran could reduce growth in the euro area by 0.5 percentage points in 2026.

A unified Middle East maritime coalition on its own would neither reverse these trends nor fully restore freedom of navigation. But it would be an important first step in denying Tehran opportunities to drive wedges between long-standing allies and partners. If, instead, the current trajectory of political discord, piecemeal missions, and short-term adaptation by commercial shippers continues, Iran and the Houthis will learn that they can exploit divisions among foreign governments, selectively escalating maritime threats to extract concessions. And other U.S. adversaries will learn the same lesson—that economic disruption is an extraordinarily effective weapon when the world lacks the will to defend its commons.

#6008. Talarico campaigns alongside Democrat who called ICE 'new KKK' and demanded its abolition

Fox News host Will Cain discusses accusations from James Talarico’s former classmate Mike Garcia about the Democratic Texas Senate candidate's honesty on 'The Will Cain Show.'

James Talarico, a U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, briefly praised Frederick Haynes III, a Democratic congressional candidate who compared President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts to the KKK, at a get-out-the-vote event on Thursday as part of his Clear Eyes Full Hearts tour.

"Give it up for your next congressman, Dr. Freddy Haynes. Thank you, Dr. Haynes, for those kind words and for your service to this community," Talarico said, following an introduction and speech from Haynes.

Although Talarico has not issued a formal endorsement of Haynes, the moment is notable for Talarico as he pitches himself as a Democrat who can represent the values of the Republican-leaning Lone Star State — and as he tries to distance himself from controversy over past remarks Republicans have characterized as woke.

TALARICO RALLY WARMUP ACT CALLS FOR ABOLISHING ICE, CONTRASTING SENATE HOPEFUL'S MESSAGE

State Representative James Talarico addresses the crowd during a campaign rally after launching his Senate campaign for the seat currently held by John Cornyn in Round Rock, Texas, Sept. 9, 2025. (Callaghan O'Hare for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Haynes, the pastor of Friendship-West Baptist Church, has framed many of his political views in the context of race and did so again on the event with Talarico.

"You transformed ICE into the new KKK and brought about terror in this nation," Haynes said of Trump's use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"It’s time to melt ICE. It’s time to abolish ICE," Haynes added.

Haynes is running to fill the seat of Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, the incumbent in Texas' 30th Congressional District who gave up her seat in a Senate bid she ultimately lost. During his campaign, Haynes has framed his support for climate policy as a fight against "environmental racism." He has also accused conservatives and the Trump administration of benefiting from fears of Black advancement.

"They have used Black people and perceived Black progress as the boogeyman. We have not witnessed this kind of corruption, this kind of blatant corruption," Haynes said in an October interview.

"We are witnessing the demolishing of what democratic infrastructure was built by the gains of the civil rights movement," Haynes added.

Even before his congressional run, Haynes made political commentary that relied heavily on a racial lens.

After the death of Charlie Kirk, a conservative political commentator who started Turning Point USA, Haynes described Kirk as a man with views "rooted in White supremacy" and contrasted it with the deaths of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.

"A White Christian gets killed, murdered — not assassinated. We going to tell the whole truth today. Martin King got assassinated. Malcolm X got assassinated. Medgar Evers got assassinated. Don’t compare Kirk to King," Haynes said in a September 2025 address to his church.

UN PUSHES NATIONS TO CONSIDER SLAVERY REPARATIONS BUT LEGAL GROUP SAYS IDEA 'NOT GOING TO FLY IN THE US'

Rev. Frederick Douglass Haynes III, a Dallas megachurch pastor and social activist, is running to replace Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, in Texas Congressional District 30. (Fox News)

Haynes would go on to condemn Kirk's death and political violence.

Haynes has also said he was a personal supporter of reparations.

"America, you owe us. What you done to us has been immoral. It’s been evil. It’s been unjust. It’s been downright wrong and the only way to bring salvation to America — you gotta pay us what you owe us," Haynes said at a Solidarity for Reparations event at a San Francisco church.

"I've come by to say, San Francisco, California, Texas, United States of America, if you want salvation to come to this house, you've got to engage in reparations."

For his own part, Talarico has also supported the idea of reparations, framing it as an outflow of his religious convictions.

"Reparations, repairing past harms, is part of my faith tradition. It’s part of the values I was raised with," Talarico said in a town hall meeting in July. "We have to correct the injustices of our past."

In the closing days of his campaign, Talarico has argued that, despite some of his views on race and gender which run counter to conservative stances, he could still represent Texas as a moderate.

TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS

Frederick Haynes III is running to replace outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. He is a megachurch pastor in Dallas who Crockett has cited as "my pastor." (Haynes for Congress)

"Our campaign has been able to show that you can be a more moderate, reasonable candidate and still be exciting," Talarico said in October.

Talarico’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment if his comment about Haynes should be viewed as an endorsement of his platform or his views on race in politics.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

#6007. Russia the Disruptor
